title: New in AWS Quick: More capable flows, an updated web experience, and agents that work together
abstract: Turn one person’s process into your team’s process, get more done in the Quick web app, and get more complete answers from agents working together. AWS Quick is the AI workspace built only for work. Today, we are releasing updates that help your team get more of its everyday work done: Build, see, and improve business processes, all through conversation. Describe a process in chat and Quick builds a flow to orchestrate agents, skills, and tools with access to structured data, knowledge, and apps. New deterministic steps help make your workflows consistent and verifiable, now with longer-running workflows and support for large data volumes. Triage your day and keep agents working in the Quick web app. The updated web app puts what needs your attention and a daily briefing on your home screen, adds the agents and skills you use on desktop, and keeps your work running after you close the tab. Complete work spanning multiple agents through a single prompt. With multi-agent orchestration, several specialized agents work on your request at the same time, and Quick combines what they find into one response. Bring more of your data into Quick. Connect to Meta ads and Amplitude, then ask in natural language and combine the answers with your other sources. Skills on web, security and governance improvements, and more languages: Turn the way you do a task into a skill Quick can reuse, now in the Quick web app. Set configurable content safety and sensitive-information controls for user prompts. Support for Japanese, German, Chinese (Simplified and Traditional), and Vietnamese. AI assistants make individuals faster, but the gains often stay with one person. The way one analyst builds the monthly report rarely becomes the way the team builds it, and work waits until someone is back at their desk. This release helps your team turn what one person knows into a process everyone can rely on, and keeps work moving when you step away. Turn one person’s process into your team’s process AWS Quick Flows already helps teams automate and standardize business processes so people can focus on their most important work. Now you can build, run, and refine flows entirely in chat. And your flows can take on more of your tough work, whether you start it from the web, desktop, or mobile app. For example, here is how flows could support a finance team. Maya is a financial planning and analysis manager at a retailer. Each month, she prepares a report for her VP of Finance that explains changes to costs and margins. For each region, she pulls last month’s results, compares them to the plan in a spreadsheet, writes commentary on the biggest changes, and sends the report. The process lives in her memory and a personal checklist. When she is out, a teammate has to rebuild the report from scratch, and it looks different every time. With Quick, Maya can standardize the process, automate it, and make it available to her team. She describes her process in chat, the way she would explain it to a new employee. Quick builds the flow from her description and she tests and refines it in the same conversation. A diagram beside the chat shows each step, so she can confirm it matches how she works. title: Cut self-hosted LLM cost and latency with the distributed KV caching agent skill
abstract: Customers increasingly self-host large language models (LLMs) on GPUs for control over cost, accuracy, and latency. However, self-hosting often means paying for redundant GPU work because small, isolated caches on each server can’t hold or share the growing context AI agents and chat applications resend. Consider a legal AI assistant that can accumulate hundreds of thousands of tokens of case history in each conversation. When a lawyer returns to a thread after lunch, responses from the LLM can take minutes. The GPU server that picks up the request has none of that history in its memory. So, the GPU recomputes the key-value (KV) attention states for all of those tokens, a step called prefill, before it writes a word. The same pattern slows down resumed coding agents, agentic AI assistants, and document Q&A assistants. Distributed KV caching with Amazon ElastiCache can cut self-hosted LLM inference costs by up to 40% and time to first token (TTFT) by up to 80%. Distributed KV caching extends GPU-local caches with a shared tier beside your GPU fleet so any server can reuse KV state for days across sessions, routing shifts, and server failures. “ Announcing distributed KV caching for self-hosted LLMs with Amazon ElastiCache ” dives into the technical details and the performance benchmarks. This post details the distributed KV caching skill in the Agent Toolkit for AWS. With this skill, you can evaluate and set up distributed KV caching from within your coding agent in a few prompts. The skill guides the agent through checking whether your workload benefits from distributed KV caching, setting up a cache cluster for testing or production workload, and troubleshooting your LLM inference caching. The skill works with Kiro , Claude Code, OpenAI Codex, and other coding agents that support Agent Skills. We walk through how the skill works with four conversations: diagnosing a slow first token, sizing and pricing the cache, setting it up, and fixing a failed transfer. Why a skill for KV caching and what can it do? The benefits for your workload depend on characteristics such as LLM models used, user traffic patterns, and prompt routing choices, and can be complex to estimate. We created the KVTrace tool to get close estimates of the benefits for your workload, from your own model and traffic before you deploy any infrastructure, at no additional charge. The skill simplifies this evaluation and the setup, and guides your coding agent through the following best practices before changing anything: A fit check before any spend. The agent reads your GPU fleet with a read-only describe-instances call and counts Elastic Fabric Adapter (EFA) interfaces. It asks only for what it can’t see: engine, model, tensor-parallel (TP) size, KV data type, server price, and how often prompts repeat. It stops and explains when something doesn’t fit. Numbers from your workload. For short prompts, loading KV state can take longer than computing it again. Above a certain prompt length (the cutover point), the read wins. That cutover and how often your prompts repeat decide whether the cache is worth its price. The agent estimates savings from your own traffic with KVTrace, at no additional charge, and stops if they don’t cover the cache’s cost. Every number says where it came from. Manage configuration across inference servers with the stack you already run. It keeps your routing and the engine’s settings and sets the servers in your inference fleet to one KV ID mechanism (hash and seed) and an explicit KV data type. Matching settings avoid key mismatches, where each server writes KV state the others can’t find. Implements best practices. title: Introducing managed cluster extensions for observability and user management in Amazon SageMaker HyperPod Slurm
abstract: Keeping a shared Slurm cluster for foundation model development in sync entails keeping several separately maintained pieces of configuration matched to what’s running on the nodes. The cluster’s shape lives on multiple configuration files, its software in custom scripts, its network topology in files that must be edited as nodes change, and its users in a roster that an administrator must maintain and rerun. Over time these pieces drift away from what’s actually running, and nothing tells you when they do. We believe cluster configurations should be managed the way you manage the rest of your AWS infrastructure. You declare what you want through an API or the console, AWS validates it before it’s applied, the cluster is kept in that state continuously, and you can see whether it’s working. During 2026, Amazon SageMaker HyperPod brought that approach to Slurm clusters, with API-driven Slurm configuration, AMI-based configuration, continuous provisioning, automatic topology management, and deep health checks. Today, we launched cluster extensions, which bring the same approach to the software and settings on running nodes, with managed extensions for observability and user management. However, through all of it, you still keep full access to every node in your cluster, including the controller node. You can SSH in, configure nodes directly, and run your own lifecycle scripts. The APIs give you less to maintain, direct access gives you more control, and you choose the balance. In this post, we walk through the features we introduced in 2026 and explain why the software on running nodes needed a different mechanism. We then show how cluster extensions work, through both the API and the console, and follow a platform team through a quarter on a cluster that uses them. A declarative foundation for Slurm cluster operations We can think of a Slurm cluster’s configuration grouped into six layers. Five of them describe the cluster itself: its definition, node setup, capacity, network topology, and hardware health. The sixth covers the software running on its nodes, which we discuss in the next section. The following figure shows the six layers. Earlier in 2026, we brought declarative management to the first five layers. With API-driven Slurm configuration , administrators define node roles, partitions, and Amazon FSx for Lustre and Amazon FSx for OpenZFS mounts in CreateCluster and UpdateCluster requests, and connect an external accounting database . HyperPod updates partition settings while preserving other controller-node Slurm customizations. AMI-based configuration replaces routine setup scripts with images preconfigured with Slurm, Docker, Enroot, Pyxis, and home directories. A custom AMI or OnInitComplete script handles organization-specific software. Continuous provisioning for Slurm retries capacity requests in the background; AMI-based configuration works with it , minimum capacity requirements let teams specify MinInstanceCount, and cluster operations track scaling requests. Automatic topology management maintains the network layout as nodes scale or are replaced. On Slurm 25.11 or later, partition-level topology supports tree or block topology per partition. For hardware health, on-demand deep health checks stress GPUs and test NVIDIA Collective Communications Library (NCCL) connectivity, while deep health checks with continuous provisioning run as nodes are provisioned. Nodes under check stay in Slurm maintenance reservations until checks finish, keeping jobs off them. Introducing cluster extensions The five layers described so far are configurations that HyperPod can derive or apply once, when it provisions a node. The sixth layer, the software that runs on the nodes, behaves differently because it keeps changing for the life of the cluster. title: Introducing Amazon SageMaker HyperPod Global Inference Gateway: One endpoint across Regions and clusters
abstract: During a traffic peak, a request can sit in a queue on a saturated HyperPod cluster while GPUs on another cluster, sometimes in another AWS Region, sit idle. You have already paid for that capacity, but your requests can’t reach it. In Introducing Amazon SageMaker HyperPod Inference Gateway , we showed how the Inference Gateway gives each Amazon SageMaker HyperPod cluster a single, GPU-aware endpoint. It reads real-time signals such as key-value (KV) cache utilization and queue depth to place every request on the best-suited pod. That solves routing inside one cluster, but not across clusters. Today, SageMaker HyperPod introduces the Global Inference Gateway. It is one SageMaker-managed gateway that routes across every cluster you register, in one Region or across Regions. The gateway picks the cluster and carries the request over the AWS backbone, with automatic failover and authentication through AWS Signature Version 4 (SigV4) and AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM). Inside each cluster, the Inference Gateway keeps picking the pod, unchanged. The Global Inference Gateway is the second tier of the architecture we described in part 1. The challenge: Capacity spread across clusters and Regions Models are getting larger, and the GPU capacity to serve them is harder to find. To get enough of it, you spread it across more clusters and more Regions. Consider a team that serves four models across five HyperPod clusters in two Regions. Without the Inference Gateway, clients track 20 endpoints: one per model per cluster. The Inference Gateway cuts that to five, one per cluster. But each client still picks a cluster itself. That choice has costs: Uneven load. During peaks, requests queue in one Region while GPUs in the other Region are idle. Manual failover. When a cluster fails, an engineer changes configuration to move traffic away from it. Custom plumbing. Spreading traffic across Regions means building and maintaining load balancers, DNS, and cross-Region networking yourself. The team needs one endpoint that sends each request to the best-suited cluster and moves traffic off a failed cluster on its own. Key benefits The Global Inference Gateway helps you get more from the GPU capacity you already have, with less to operate. Put idle GPUs to work. During a peak, requests overflow to clusters with available capacity in the same Region or another one, instead of queuing on a saturated cluster. Fail over automatically. When a cluster fails, the gateway moves its traffic to the next-best cluster. Clients don’t change anything. Use one endpoint for everything. Clients call a single SageMaker-managed endpoint instead of tracking one endpoint per cluster or per model. Skip the custom networking. You don’t build or maintain load balancers, DNS, or cross-Region networking. Stay private by default. Every request is authenticated with SigV4 and IAM, and it reaches your clusters only over AWS PrivateLink. Customer feedback “At Bagelcode, we run our own LLM inference service on AWS to help teams across the company, including our game teams, use AI to improve how they work. In our beta tests, the Global Inference Gateway in Amazon SageMaker HyperPod routed requests across two AWS Regions through a single endpoint and kept serving them when one cluster could no longer serve the model. title: How Standard Bank Group automates AI risk assessment for generative AI
abstract: This post is co-written with Tala Qraitem from AWS and Jörg Fischer from Standard Bank Group Having an AI policy is one thing. Proving, one use case at a time, that AI systems follow it is another. Every new generative AI application adds one more system to prove. Teams can now build one in days, but each still needs a risk committee’s approval before it reaches customers or employees. When that approval depends on reviewers reading documents and testing the system by hand, governance becomes the slowest step in the pipeline. Standard Bank Group chose to automate that proof. Working with AWS Professional Services, the bank deployed an automated assessment that scores each generative AI use case against international AI standards and its own policies. The assessment produces reports and a dashboard that show what is already in place, what is working well, and what still needs mitigation. This post explains how the assessment runs on AWS and what Standard Bank Group learned from its first runs. Governing AI with the framework you already have Standard Bank Group didn’t need a new AI policy. Like most large banks, it already had an established model risk practice that covers concerns such as explainability and fairness, and a change risk process that assesses each new use case according to its level of risk before it goes live. Generative AI increases the complexity, because models and tooling change every three to six months, yet each use case still needs to meet the same high security and compliance bar. “At Standard Bank, this assessment demonstrates how we are working with AWS to embed intelligent, automated risk management into our AI journey, allowing us to accelerate meaningful business value while maintaining the trust and controls that banking demands. We believe responsible AI is not about slowing innovation down but enabling it to build and scale with confidence.” — Jörg Fischer, Group Chief Information and AI Officer, Standard Bank Group The goal was to automate evidence gathering and testing, then feed the results into the approval gates Standard Bank Group already runs. Review and approval stay with the risk committee, but the committee now bases each decision on consistent evidence, collected the same way across use cases. How the assessment works Figure 1 shows how the assessment’s components fit together in Standard Bank Group’s AWS account, from intake through evaluation to reporting. Figure 1: The assessment pipeline in Standard Bank Group’s AWS account, from intake through evaluation to reporting The assessment runs entirely in Standard Bank Group’s own AWS account. Documents, code, and test results stay in an Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) bucket there. The AWS Well-Architected Tool handles intake, AWS Step Functions orchestrates the pipeline, and a foundation model on Amazon Bedrock evaluates the evidence. It uses a technique called LLM-as-a-judge, in which a large language model checks evidence against defined criteria. With Amazon Bedrock, Standard Bank Group could use a foundation model without stepping outside the controls it already runs on AWS. The bank controls access to the model through AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM), just as it does for its other AWS workloads. Amazon Bedrock doesn’t share the bank’s prompts or model outputs with model providers, and doesn’t use them to train models. Because Amazon Bedrock offers many foundation models through one API, the team can move to a newer judge model by changing a configuration setting instead of rebuilding the pipeline. Each assessment moves through four steps. In the first two, a pre-assessment agent collects evidence about the use case, then the pipeline examines it and tests the application directly. The third evaluates that evidence against controls. The fourth summarizes the results in a standard, predefined format and delivers them to the people who act on them. title: Announcing Amazon Textract Insights: Verifiable generative AI for documents
abstract: Organizations across financial services, insurance, healthcare, and the public sector depend on document processing. They turn scanned files and paper forms into structured data their systems can act on. As generative AI has matured, these organizations want more than accurate text extraction. They want to describe the information they need in their own words and get dependable, auditable answers from complex documents. Today, we are announcing the general availability of Amazon Textract Insights , a new generative AI feature of Amazon Textract available through a new API within Amazon Textract. With Amazon Textract Insights, you describe the fields you want in natural language and submit a document or a mixed, multi-document packet. You receive structured results in which each value carries a confidence score and page-level grounding, with no model training required. The challenge of extracting data from mixed packets Many of the high-value document workloads involve diverse, mixed packets rather than clean, single-purpose files. A mortgage file, for example, typically arrives as a single scan holding a W-2, payslips, bank statements, and a page of handwritten notes. Each has its own layout and appears in no fixed order. Claims files and onboarding packages can look very similar: typed forms, dense tables, scanned receipts, and free-text letters interleaved in one file. Teams usually take one of two approaches, and each has trade-offs. The first is a custom pipeline that combines optical character recognition, document splitting, classification, a foundation model prompt, and a review step. The team must integrate, scale, and operate all of it. The second is a general-purpose large language model used by default. It returns fluent answers but does not reliably cite the source page or give a confidence score. Without a traceable source and a calibrated score, it is hard to know which values to accept automatically and which to review. This uncertainty often limits how far teams can automate. Amazon Textract Insights is built for reliable document processing, bringing this entire workflow into a single asynchronous request on Amazon Textract. Rather than assembling and operating a custom pipeline, your team works through one managed API and moves directly to the data it needs. How Amazon Textract Insights works With Amazon Textract Insights, you define what to extract in a blueprint. A blueprint is a JSON Schema in which each field carries a natural language description of what to find. Each field also has an inference type that determines whether the value is read verbatim from the page or inferred from the content of the document. You can begin with an AWS public blueprint for a common document type, such as a W-2, Form 1040, Form 1098, a passport, or a birth certificate. You can also author your own blueprint for the documents specific to your business. For a mixed packet, you add the blueprints for each document type you expect to the same project. You then submit a single file of up to 3,000 pages from your own Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) bucket and enable splitting. Amazon Textract Insights splits the packet into logical sub-documents, matches each one to the blueprint that fits it, extracts the requested fields, and returns a confidence score and grounding for each value. For example, suppose you receive a mortgage application as a single 26-page PDF that contains a W-2, payslips, bank statements, and a loan officer’s handwritten notes. You create an Amazon Textract Insights project with the AWS public W-2, payslip, and bank statement blueprints, add a custom blueprint for loan officer notes, and enable splitting. You then submit the file from your Amazon S3 bucket with a single StartDocumentInsights call. Amazon Textract Insights splits the file into its individual documents, matches each one to its blueprint, and writes the results to your S3 bucket. title: Introducing enhanced infrastructure observability in Amazon SageMaker HyperPod
abstract: Large-scale model training is one of the most expensive workloads you can run on GPUs, and a single unhealthy accelerator can stall an entire distributed job. When training throughput drops, the hard part is rarely noticing that something is wrong. It is figuring out why and where. Teams often spend hours or days sifting through logs and disconnected dashboards to decide whether a slowdown came from a throttled GPU, a saturated network link, or a stalled data pipeline on the host. Today, we are announcing enhanced observability in Amazon SageMaker HyperPod, a new capability that helps you diagnose GPU training issues faster. It brings together diagnostic and profiling capabilities for training workloads that run on both Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS) and Slurm orchestrators: Diagnostic summary uses Amazon CloudWatch’s DetectGroupOutliers API to compare each GPU in a training job on utilization, memory, temperature, power, and SM clock, and flags GPUs that deviate from their peers. Static diagnostic rules surface common failure patterns such as GPU hardware faults (XID errors, ECC memory errors), EFA throughput drops, thermal throttling, and overheating, so you catch degradation before it affects training. Why you need it Distributed training is expensive, and small inefficiencies compound into significant wasted GPU hours. Until now, getting visibility into HyperPod infrastructure meant stitching together separate tools, and even then, the metrics told you that performance had degraded without telling you why. Enhanced observability closes three gaps. It isolates a single bad accelerator across hundreds or thousands of GPUs whether through XID errors, ECC memory faults, or thermal throttling, so you spend time on the fix instead of the search. Together, these capabilities reduce troubleshooting time and help you keep expensive accelerators busy. How it works Each capability targets a different layer of a distributed training job. Default and advanced metrics Enhanced observability collects telemetry at two levels: Default metrics (enabled automatically) cover cluster health, CPU/disk/OS-level usage, GPU utilization and temperature, and per-job resource utilization. These metrics are collected every 30 seconds and sent to your chosen metric store with approximately 1–2% CPU overhead and 250–300 MB of memory. Advanced metrics (opt-in) provide deeper visibility: Full node exporter suite: comprehensive host-level metrics. All NVIDIA GPU DCGM and AWS Neuron metrics: detailed accelerator telemetry including clock speeds, power, PCIe activity, and error indicators. Elastic Fabric Adapter (EFA) metrics: network interface throughput, drops, retransmissions, and errors. Advanced metrics are optional because they increase the volume of telemetry sent to your metric store, which has a cost implication. Most customers running small jobs on small clusters may not need them, but they are essential for long-running training jobs on large clusters where patterns emerge over time. Metric stores You can choose between two metric stores: Amazon CloudWatch (new default) provides native monitoring through CloudWatch SageMaker Insights, so you can visualize metrics without leaving the AWS Management Console. Amazon Managed Service for Prometheus for teams that standardize on Prometheus and Grafana for observability. Previously, only Prometheus was supported. CloudWatch is now the default, offering lower pricing compared to Amazon Managed Service Prometheus and tighter integration with the SageMaker console. Diagnostic summary The diagnostic summary uses two complementary approaches to surface issues across your HyperPod cluster. GPU outlier detection uses CloudWatch’s DetectGroupOutliers API to compare GPUs within a training job across utilization, memory usage, temperature, power draw, and SM clock frequency. title: Amazon SageMaker Inference: 2026 launches in review, part 2
abstract: From first endpoint to global fleet: 14 more launches for managed endpoints and HyperPod Inference In September, Amazon SageMaker Inference: 2026 year-to-date launches in review covered 13 launches that shortened the path from a model to a production endpoint. Most of them answered one question: how do I get this model serving quickly and reliably? This post covers the 13 launches that came next, bringing the total for 2026 to 26. Once a model is in production, the questions change. Teams want to know which configuration the model should run on now that traffic is real, how to fit more models onto GPUs they already pay for, what to do when the next model is too large for one machine, why requests wait in one Region while GPUs sit idle in another, and why latency rose when nobody changed anything. This post takes those questions in the order teams usually meet them. For HyperPod Inference, it listed additional routing strategies, broader support for model serving frameworks, and expanded multi-Region networking. The Inference Gateway and the Global Inference Gateway deliver the routing and multi-Region work, and managed NVIDIA Dynamo is a new serving framework. For managed endpoints, the roadmap pointed to deeper integration with the rest of the AWS AI landscape. Inference recommendations now run from Amazon SageMaker AI Studio, the SageMaker Python SDK, and the coding agents engineers already use, and endpoints can now route requests across Regions and accounts. To keep each section concrete, we follow one hypothetical team through the blog post. In the spring, they launched a customer support assistant on a 70B-parameter model behind a single SageMaker AI endpoint, using the launches from part 1. By the fall, they need to support more product lines, adopt a larger reasoning model, serve customers in a second Region, and keep their GPU bill flat. The launches at a glance Figure 1: The five stages in this post and the launches in each Choose the right configuration from wherever you work The team picked its first configuration from a benchmark run in April. Since then, they have added four LoRA (Low-Rank Adaptation) adapters, one for each product line, and the product team has set a target of 500 milliseconds for time to first token (TTFT) at peak load. The April configuration was never tested against either change. The engineers who will re-run the analysis work in notebooks and coding agents, and few of them use the console. Inference recommendations launched in April as an API. Four updates since then make it available in more of the places teams work, and let it answer two harder questions: how many adapters an endpoint can carry, and how much concurrency it can take before it misses a latency target. A new agent skill brings the same expertise into coding agents. Inference recommendations in SageMaker AI Studio (July 2026) Blog: Launching UI for generative AI inference recommendations in Amazon SageMaker AI The April launch automated instance, container, and optimization selection through APIs. Inference recommendations are now also available in SageMaker AI Studio as a guided, low-code workflow. In Studio, choose Jobs , then Inference optimization . Choose a use-case profile (Interact, Generate, Summarize, or Custom), an optimization goal (minimize latency, maximize throughput, or minimize cost), and a model from SageMaker JumpStart, Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3), the Model Registry, or an existing SageMaker model. SageMaker AI benchmarks candidate configurations on real GPU infrastructure using NVIDIA AIPerf and applies techniques that match the goal, such as speculative decoding for throughput or kernel tuning for latency. You compare the ranked results by TTFT, inter-token latency, throughput, and cost, and then deploy the chosen configuration to a real-time endpoint from Studio. title: Use Kimi Code CLI with models on Amazon Bedrock
abstract: Kimi Code CLI is an open source coding agent from Moonshot AI, the creator of the Kimi series of open-weight foundation models. Previously, using Kimi Code with models on Amazon Bedrock meant configuring a generic connection “provider” with an Amazon Bedrock API key. For many AWS customers, this meant introducing an extra credential to obtain and protect. With v2.7.0, Moonshot AI adds a native bedrock provider to the CLI. You can now configure the agent to use your standard AWS credential chain, including named profiles and single sign-on (SSO), instead of creating and managing a separate API key. In this post, we show you how to connect Kimi Code CLI to models on Amazon Bedrock using your existing AWS credentials. We use Kimi K3.1 Pro Highspeed as an example, which supports streaming, configurable reasoning, image input, and client-side tool calling. What’s new Amazon Bedrock provides pay-per-token inference for a range of open and proprietary models from leading providers, available through standard APIs . Processing stays within the AWS data boundary, as detailed in the Data protection section of the User Guide. The model cards detail which APIs and features are supported for each model. In older versions of the Kimi Code CLI, you could connect to Amazon Bedrock through a provider with type = "openai" or type = "openai_responses" . These use the OpenAI-compatible Chat Completions or Responses APIs, respectively. This approach required you to set the regional base_url and provide an Amazon Bedrock API key . The key could be short-term or long-term, but it was a separate credential for you to obtain and manage. The native provider changes that setup: Use your existing AWS authentication workflow. The bedrock provider can resolve temporary credentials through the standard AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI) credential chain. You can use the default chain or select a named profile, including a profile backed by SSO. Override the protocol for each model, if needed. The provider infers an API format and regional endpoint from the model ID, but you can change them as detailed in the “Override endpoint URL and protocol” section of this post. AWS recommends short-term credentials over long-term credentials. This new path reduces reliance on manually managed API keys, but it doesn’t change your responsibility to protect AWS credentials and scope permissions appropriately. How it works The native provider handles authentication and request routing in four steps: Resolve AWS credentials. Unless you configure an Amazon Bedrock API key, the bedrock provider uses the standard AWS credential chain in your environment. You can set AWS_PROFILE to select a specific named profile . Generate a short-lived bearer token. The provider uses @aws/bedrock-token-generator to create a short-term Amazon Bedrock API key, and renews it when necessary. You don’t need to place any AWS access key or manually generated Amazon Bedrock key in the Kimi Code config.toml . However, an explicit key given through api_key or api_key_env takes precedence if you provide it. Build the regional endpoint. The provider resolves AWS_REGION or AWS_DEFAULT_REGION and constructs the appropriate bedrock-runtime endpoint for the model’s inferred API. For Kimi models, this resolves to the recommended OpenAI-compatible Chat Completions path. Call the selected inference profile. The model alias maps to an Amazon Bedrock model or inference profile ID. This example uses the global inference profile global.moonshotai.kimi-k3.1 . The global. prefix selects the profile, while AWS_REGION determines the regional endpoint that receives your request. The CLI then streams the model response and can use the model’s client-side tool-calling support during coding tasks. Authentication, authorization, model access, and network connectivity must all succeed for a request to complete. title: Enable AI agents to pay for AWS Marketplace x402 products with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore payments
abstract: When Amazon Bedrock AgentCore payments became generally available in August 2026, agents could autonomously pay for paid APIs, MCP servers, and web content over open protocols like x402 and MPP with payment limits and full observability. Today we extend that autonomy to AWS Marketplace , so agents can discover and buy x402-enabled software, APIs, data, and content, and pay in USD on the agent developer’s AWS bill, removing the need for stablecoin wallets or API keys. Figure 1: Overview of AgentCore payments showing the new AWS Billing integration for purchasing on AWS Marketplace Developers can also configure and automate discovery through the AWS Marketplace connector in AgentCore Gateway . Existing guardrails carry over, developers can set spending limits and approved sellers using AgentCore policy, and the payment session cap is enforced by AgentCore payments, so an agent is unable to overspend. Transactions are auditable in AWS CloudTrail and AWS Cost Explorer . Because agent purchases run through AWS accounts on both sides, agentic purchasing meets the security and auditability enterprises expect. The x402 catalog on AWS Marketplace is expanding with a growing roster of trusted, verified sellers. Tavily, a live search provider for agentic commerce, is one of them: Agentic commerce isn’t just about giving agents the ability to pay. It’s about giving enterprises the confidence to let them. That conviction is driving Tavily’s collaboration with the AWS team on the design of Agentic Commerce. By bringing secure, x402 powered transactions to AWS Marketplace and connecting agents with trusted, KYC verified providers, AWS is laying the foundation for autonomous commerce at production scale. This is what enterprise ready agentic commerce looks like. — Rotem Weiss, Founder & CEO, Tavily What’s launching today Today’s launch adds AWS Billing as a payment option in AgentCore payments. An agent can now pay x402-enabled AWS Marketplace sellers per request, in USD, settling on their AWS bill. When an AWS Marketplace seller responds with 402 Payment Required, its response includes a signed quote for the purchase. With AWS Billing, the agent can forward the seller’s x402 response to AgentCore payments. AgentCore payments checks session budgets, then returns a payment token. The agent retries the request to the seller with the payment token included and receives a successful response. AWS bills the charge to the AWS account where Payment Manager is set up, and the charge appears on that account’s AWS bill. To set up AWS Marketplace purchasing, the developer creates a Payment Manager with an AWS Billing connector. The connector only requires you to set up a service-linked role to access AWS Marketplace. Then, for each task, developers can create a payment session with a spending limit and give the agent the session ID. An agent’s first purchase from a seller creates an agreement for the AWS account with that seller, and AWS Marketplace automatically tracks later purchases against it. Each product will then show up as an AWS Marketplace line item. If your organization uses Private Marketplace , agents can only buy the products it allows. In addition, to discover new sellers, we are launching a new AWS Marketplace connector in AgentCore Gateway . This optional integration helps agents find products and their endpoints. At launch, AWS Billing supports the x402 exact scheme, where the seller quotes a fixed price for each request. In this post, we walk through a research agent that discovers a tool, pays for a single request through AWS Billing, and answers with sources, with nothing set up in advance. We also provide an accompanying GitHub sample that you can use to evaluate the setup in your own AWS account. title: How the BMW Group governs hundreds of agents across thousands of developers
abstract: When hundreds of agents serve thousands of developers, enterprise governance can’t be an afterthought. At the BMW Group’s R&D, more than 12,500 developers work on approximately 500 million lines of vehicle software code. This software is augmented by the BMW Connected Vehicle backend, a cloud-based system of more than 1,300 microservices providing digital services for 24 million vehicles in the field. In regulated industry, the bar for (software) quality, stability, and governance compliance is exceptionally high. While research, frameworks, and guidelines now facilitate building agents, industrializing and operating high-quality agents in an efficient, scalable manner remains a significant challenge. Scaling agentic AI across a large organization cannot be achieved by isolated teams. It requires collective effort, locally driven experimentation, and active knowledge sharing across the enterprise. This creates a fundamental governance dichotomy: Development teams need the freedom to innovate rapidly, while the enterprise must enforce standards for safety, security, composability, and cost-efficiency. Without that balance, organizations risk a fragmented landscape of AI islands and costly duplicate work. This presents a real challenge given hundreds of globally distributed teams building agents across the BMW Group. In this post, we detail the practices and patterns that support BMW’s R&D teams in building, governing and operating agents at scale without sacrificing speed, quality or compliance. Solution Our premise is straightforward: build agents that can cooperate from the start. This requires an architecture that makes diversity composable, governable, and automatable, without requiring a single framework or toolchain. Central to this architecture is the agent harness, a runtime layer wrapped around a large language model (LLM). It provides the execution loop, tool dispatch, memory management, and observability hooks for autonomous operation. Just as the AWS Well-Architected Framework standardized cloud infrastructure design, agentic systems need equivalent patterns, reusable blueprints encoding governance, composability, and operational best practices from the start. We organize our solution around five interlocking practices, drawn from hands-on experience building and operating agentic systems at enterprise scale since 2023. Each practice is codified as infrastructure as code (IaC), making adoption repeatable, auditable, and enforceable across teams without blocking DevOps velocity. Govern proactively, not retroactively Governance must be structural from the start and maintained across the full lifecycle. We advocate for three properties of effective agentic governance: Framework-agnostic and externalized: Governance rules such as authentication, authorization, rate limiting and content filtering are enforced at the integration layer. This includes a Model Context Protocol (MCP) gateway, a central agent registry and orchestration boundary, rather than within individual agent codebases. This means governance survives framework migrations, model swaps, and team reorganizations. Domain-sensitive and graduated: Not every agent action carries the same risk: drafting documentation, updating customer records, and production database writes demand very different levels of oversight. We implement graduated trust through per-step autonomy levels: Level 0 (Human-in-the-loop): Every action requires explicit human approval. This is the starting point for new agents and high-risk operations. Level 1 (Human-on-the-loop): The agent executes autonomously but surfaces decisions for asynchronous human review. Suitable for medium-risk tasks with defined inputs, outputs, and rollback options. Level 2 (Autonomous within guardrails): The agent operates independently within strictly defined policy boundaries, enforced deterministically rather than through prompt instructions (see below). title: Run your whole selling business in AWS Quick
abstract: Most sellers do not need another AI product to learn. They need the tools and information they already use brought together, so they can see what is happening in their business and act on it. AWS Quick and the Amazon Selling Partner plugin do that together. Quick brings an Amazon seller’s sales data, inventory signals, and marketplace intelligence into one place, where questions become answers and answers become actions. It understands the seller’s full business context, so the seller does not need to re-explain their catalog, their margins, or their competitive landscape in every conversation. It is built on AWS, the same infrastructure Amazon uses to run its own marketplace. At Amazon Accelerate on September 23, 2026, Amazon announced the Selling Partner plugin and launched it in beta in AWS Quick. This post covers what launched, how to claim the free AWS Quick offer, and what the experience looks like day to day. It also covers how the skills and connectors work when a seller puts them to use. Limited-time offer: 12 months of AWS Quick Plus, free. Every primary selling account holder worldwide can claim a free 12-month subscription, plus access for 10 additional users you delegate. Sign up by December 31, 2026. Claim your free AWS Quick Plus offer. 1. Why Quick is right for Amazon sellers Four things make Quick a fit for how Amazon sellers already work: it learns the business, it reaches beyond the Amazon store, it turns data into decisions, and it protects seller data on infrastructure sellers already trust. Quick knows your business, not only your prompts Quick and the Selling Partner plugin connect to a seller’s inventory feeds, sales data, and operational documents. From these, Quick builds a living understanding of the catalog structure, margin thresholds, seasonality, and competitive position. Ask Quick to audit your ASINs for Q4, and it returns a ranked recommendation built on the seller’s real margin data, historical conversion, and inventory availability. Its recommendations get sharper the more the seller works with it. Quick does not stop at your Amazon store A seller’s business runs across many tools: a storefront on another channel, an email inbox, an accounting system, spreadsheets, a supplier portal. Quick connects to where the seller already works and pulls context from across the whole operation. It is a business assistant that happens to know Amazon deeply, so the seller grows overall, not on one channel alone. It turns data into decisions you can act on Sellers are not short on data. They have Brand Analytics, Search Query Performance, advertising reports, inventory health, and listing quality data. The problem is turning those signals into one clear action. Quick does the synthesis. It watches for change, flags what matters, builds the analysis, and presents the decision with the evidence behind it. Your data stays protected on the infrastructure you already sell on Quick runs on AWS and does not use seller data to train models, not for general improvement and not for anything else. Seller data stays in the seller’s environment and never informs anyone else’s models. For a seller already operating on the Amazon marketplace, there is no new security posture to evaluate. The infrastructure is the same one protecting the seller account today, and the seller’s chosen AWS Region governs where data stays. The Amazon Selling Partner plugin The Selling Partner plugin connects AWS Quick directly to live Seller Central data. After one sign-in with a Seller Central account, the plugin gives conversational access to product listings, inventory, and sales data, pulled live rather than exported and reassembled by hand. It installs like an app, with no coding required. It ships with curated Amazon skills, and it pairs with Amazon Ads MCP so campaign performance and spend sit next to the selling data. title: Amazon SageMaker AI now detects latency drift, idle GPUs, and missed optimizations on your inference endpoints
abstract: Every inference endpoint is well tuned the day it goes into production. Teams choose an instance type, serving configuration, and scaling settings that suit the model and its traffic at launch. With the endpoint serving smoothly, they understandably move on to the next priority. The workload, however, rarely stays still. Traffic patterns evolve, prompts grow longer, serving engines such as vLLM ship new releases, SageMaker inference develops new optimization techniques, and new fine-tuned checkpoints change the resources your model needs. Over time, a well-tuned endpoint quietly drifts. Latency and time to first token edge upward. A configuration that was never quite ideal keeps missing available performance gains. A GPU provisioned for demand that never materialized sits idle week after week. Because nothing has failed, no alarm sounds, and the drift goes unnoticed until users feel it or the bill reflects it. Amazon SageMaker AI now monitors your generative AI inference endpoints and tells you when a change could improve performance or lower cost by using Generative AI optimized inference recommendations feature with Agentic experience in SageMaker JupyterLab . Monitoring is on by default for SageMaker AI inference endpoints using vLLM serving containers and GPU instances, with no setup required, and you can opt out of endpoints. SageMaker AI looks only at operational signals: latency, GPU utilization, and the endpoint’s serving configuration. It does not read your requests or responses. From those signals, it surfaces three kinds of findings: Latency drift: A week-over-week rise in median (p50) end-to-end latency or time to first token. Unused capacity: GPUs you pay for that sit mostly idle. Configuration gaps: A serving container that’s missing newer performance improvements or security patches, or an optimization such as speculative decoding or GPU kernel tuning that your model supports but the endpoint doesn’t use. SageMaker AI sends a finding through AWS Health, with one notification per endpoint that covers that endpoint’s findings. When a notification arrives, you can act on it in one place. It opens the SageMaker AI agentic experience in Amazon SageMaker Studio with the endpoint, and its recent traffic already filled in. From there, you run inference recommendations to benchmark your current configuration against alternatives and compare them side by side on response time, throughput, and cost per million tokens. That turns a judgment call into a decision backed by data. Benchmarks run on separate compute, and nothing changes on your endpoint until you choose to apply a result. In this post, we show how SageMaker AI monitors your endpoints and how to read the notifications it sends through AWS Health. We then show how to go from a notification to a benchmarked decision in SageMaker Studio. We walk through three example scenarios, show how to apply or dismiss a recommendation safely, and explain how to opt an endpoint out of monitoring. Solution overview SageMaker AI inference recommendations follow a four-step loop: observe, notify, recommend, and decide. Each step is designed so that you stay in control, and your production endpoint isn’t changed without your explicit action. Observe – Monitoring of latency and capacity usage is on by default for eligible endpoints. It doesn’t read your requests or responses, and it carries no additional GPU cost. Notify – When there is something worth acting on, you receive a plain language notification in AWS Health, plus email, explaining what was observed, why it matters, and a recommended next step. title: Inside Amazon Connect Talent: The science of structured AI interviews
abstract: For organizations hiring hundreds or thousands of people, every interview presents the same challenge: How do you give candidates a consistent opportunity to demonstrate their skills while gathering the evidence needed to make informed hiring decisions? Structured behavioral interviews offer a research-backed approach to this challenge. They use consistent, job-related questions and clear scoring criteria to give candidates an opportunity to demonstrate their skills. Decades of research in industrial-organizational (I-O) psychology have shown that structured interviews help organizations evaluate candidates and predict job performance (Schmidt & Hunter, 1998; Sackett et al., 2022). Yet delivering structured interviews at scale requires significant time and expertise to develop competencies, create q uestions, train interviewers, and evaluate responses consistently . Amazon Connect Talent brings established hiring science to AI-led interviews at scale. Connect Talent uses structured questions, adaptive follow-ups, and evidence-based scoring to help organizations gather consistent, job-related information while giving more candidates the opportunity to demonstrate their strengths. We built Connect Talent around three core design principles and evaluated how well the service applies them through a combination of internal research and independent expert review. The findings offer a closer look at the science behind Connect Talent’s AI-le d, structured interviewing. Three core design principles 1. Build interviews around job-related evidence Connect Talent builds each interview around the competencies required for the role. The service uses job requirements and established occupational frameworks to create behaviorally anchored scorecards. Each scorecard defines specific strength and concern signals, and every interview question targets the behaviors it aims to uncover. The AI interviewer also adapts to each response. After every answer, it checks whether the candidate has provided enough evidence for the competency being assessed. When details are missing, it asks targeted follow-up questions. This approach preserves the structure of the interview while giving candidates more opportunities to explain their experience. 2. Separate interviewing from scoring Connect Talent separates the interview conversation from the evaluation. The AI interviewer gathers evidence but does not assign scores. Afterward, a separate evaluation process identifies which behaviors the candidate demonstrated and cites the supporting transcript passa ges. The service calculates each competency score from 1 to 5 using a fixed formula. When the transcript lacks sufficient evidence, Connect Talent flags the competency instead of producing a score. Hiring teams can review the evidence behind each rating, and missing evidence does not automatically count against the candidate. 3. Build fairness protections into the design Connect Talent evaluates transcribed candidate responses without using video, voice tone, or physical appearance to calculate competency scores. The service also excludes candidate identity information from scoring and evaluates each competency separately. These safeguards help focus assessments on job-related behaviors and limit the influence of unrelated information. We examined whether the service generates job-relevant interview content, identifies behavioral evidence in line with expert assessments, gathers more complete responses through follow-up questions, and distinguishes between levels of demonstrated competency. title: Amazon Bedrock AgentCore harness adds Strands harness defaults, built-in tools, and lifecycle hooks
abstract: When building an AI agent, selecting a model is only the first step. The agent still needs tools, instructions for finishing the job, a way to manage context growth in long sessions, and guardrails before it executes any consequential actions, like issuing a refund. We are upgrading Amazon Bedrock AgentCore harness to use Strands harness, our open-source agent harness, released earlier this year, available under an Apache 2.0 license. AgentCore harness also introduces lifecycle hooks, so you can apply your own deterministic checks and notifications at defined points in the agent loop. With this upgrade, agents that rely on the managed defaults get a recommended model, a task-oriented system prompt, automatic prompt caching (initially for Anthropic models on Amazon Bedrock), and proactive context management. They also get additional built-in tools for planning, web retrieval, filesystem access, context offloading, and task delegation. This gives agents greater capabilities during long tasks, allowing them to keep track of subtasks, reduce context window usage, and delegate work. With hooks, you can transform non-deterministic AI behavior into predictable, safe, and governed workflows by running deterministic code at specific lifecycle checkpoints. There’s no new resource type or integration to adopt. You automatically get both updates in the AgentCore harness you already use. Strands capabilities, on AWS Strands harness provides an assembled agent foundation with recommended instructions, tools, and context management. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore harness operates that foundation as a managed AWS service. The result is a production-grade default agent that doesn’t require you to assemble and operate the harness or its infrastructure yourself. You do not need to provision compute, bundle and host the agent loop, manage session scaling, or operate tool-execution infrastructure. Each session runs in a secure, kernel-isolated microVM in AgentCore runtime, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, with managed compute, scaling, and high availability. AgentCore achieves this by connecting the harness to the services required for production agents, including session persistence, streaming responses, usage metadata, observability, AgentCore memory, Identity, Gateway, Browser, Code Interpreter, and customer-provided containers. You retain control over the model, instructions, tools, permissions, and lifecycle policies while AgentCore manages the underlying execution environment. A more capable managed harness Harness now provides a stronger experience when you use its managed defaults: A current recommended model. When you omit the model, Harness uses a recommended default model that evolves as new models are released, always keeping your harnesses up to date. Explicit harness-level and per-invocation model configurations continue to take precedence. Task-oriented instructions. The managed system prompt encourages the agent to gather relevant context, use appropriate tools, continue until the task is resolved, adapt to failures or denied actions, and verify its work before reporting completion. The default system prompt improves over time to support the latest harness behavior. Automatic prompt caching. For supported models using Converse on Amazon Bedrock, Harness caches the system prompt, tool definitions, and conversation history. Repeated calls with the same prompt and tool surface can use lower-priced cache-read tokens, reducing input processing latency and cost. Proactive context management. By default, Harness summarizes older conversation turns while retaining recent context once the context window reaches a configurable threshold. Keeping the context lean this way helps Harness run at about 34% lower token cost than other leading harnesses . Context offloading. title: Amazon Polly launches voice cloning: A unique voice for your brand
abstract: Voice cloning in Amazon Polly is now generally available as a gated release. Give Amazon Polly a few minutes of audio recordings from a speaker who has agreed to have their voice cloned, and Amazon Polly builds your own cloned voice in that speaker’s voice. The cloned voices run on the Amazon Polly generative engine, which delivers similar naturalness and accuracy as the rest of the generative voices. Amazon Polly voice cloning launches with seven languages: English, Spanish, German, French, Italian, Portuguese, and Hindi. Each cloned voice speaks the language it was recorded in. The cloned voices are automatically encrypted and access-controlled: only you can access your cloned voices. Amazon Polly voice cloning is available in all the AWS Regions supported by the Amazon Polly generative engine, including the AWS GovCloud (US) Region. Access is already enabled for select Amazon Polly customers. Others can reach out to their AWS account team or apply for access to get access. With this new feature addition, you can build the cloning lifecycle into AWS applications. Building a cloned voice is free for Amazon Polly customers, and Amazon Polly charges for cloned voice usage on a pay-as-you-go basis, see Amazon Polly Pricing page for details. Hear it for yourself Press play: the first few seconds are a real recording of the speaker, and then their cloned voice takes over with words they never recorded. From recordings to TTS voice. title: Optimize AI economics on Amazon Bedrock with Accenture’s sequenced approach
abstract: As enterprises scale AI on Amazon Bedrock , token spend often grows even as per-token prices fall. Without cost allocation tags in place, your cloud invoice shows AI spend as a single line item rather than by team, workload, agent, or model. Cheaper tokens expand adoption, and agentic workloads multiply invocations. As successful AI use cases scale, consumption can rise faster than unit prices drop. The economic question is whether the business value generated grows faster than the cost of the intelligence required to produce it. The Linux Foundation has launched the Tokenomics Foundation to develop open standards for AI cost economics, a sign that managing the economics of AI is now an industry discipline. In this post, you will learn about six levers for optimizing token spend, how Accenture applied them in production, and how to apply them using Amazon Bedrock. Accenture applied these levers in four client engagements across telecom, insurance, mining, and a large enterprise deployment. The same levers are available natively on Amazon Bedrock as described in this post. Where savings were measured, token spend fell by about 40–85 percent. Results are specific to each client’s workload and may vary. Client names are withheld by Accenture to protect client confidentiality. Attribution first: Measuring cost at the business level Before you optimize anything, you need to see where consumption is occurring, who owns it, and what business value it produces. Cost allocation tags at the team, workload, and agent level are the prerequisite for connecting consumption to accountable owners and, ultimately, to business outcomes. You apply them through Amazon Bedrock application inference profiles , one profile per application or workload, tagged by team, cost center, and environment. After you activate them as cost allocation tags in the AWS Billing and Cost Management console , you can use these tags to trace which teams, applications, and agents are driving spend. They also make it possible to measure the impact of each change you introduce. Three AWS services provide the underlying telemetry. AWS Cost and Usage Reports (CUR 2.0), delivered through AWS Data Exports , handle financial attribution, breaking down billed inference cost by workload and team after your cost allocation tags are active. Amazon CloudWatch captures operational signals such as invocation counts and latency. Amazon Bedrock model invocation logging records request-level detail, including the model used and the input and output token counts for each call. Telemetry alone isn’t enough. Engineers can read cost per invocation on a dashboard, but product owners and program leaders need a metric expressed in business terms. Accenture’s Cost per Business Transaction (CpBT) framework bridges this gap. CpBT aggregates all the model invocations, retries, tool calls, and agent handoffs that contribute to one successful business output into a single fully loaded cost figure. It surfaces the true cost of producing a result, including the failed attempts that raw token pricing hides. Tracked against the business value each workflow delivers, CpBT distinguishes a growing bill that reflects scaling success from one that reflects waste. The six optimization levers The goal of these six levers isn’t to minimize tokens at all costs. It’s to use the right amount and level of intelligence to deliver each business outcome at the appropriate cost, quality, and risk. The levers are organized into three phases based on the complexity of the change and the investment it requires. AWS and Accenture recommend working through the phases in order, and you can apply each phase independently to the workloads where it will have the most impact. title: From learning to leaderboard: How Cisco upskilled 1,200 engineers in agentic AI with AWS AI League
abstract: Cisco, like many large engineering organizations, is adopting generative and agentic AI to change how its engineers build software. The hard part is no longer access to the technology. It’s helping thousands of engineers move from watching a demo to confidently building with it. Recorded sessions and slide decks rarely close that gap. Engineers learn fastest when they build something real, see it fail, fix it, and try again. AWS designed AWS AI League for exactly that. It turns hands-on AI learning into a gamified competition, where participants customize models and build agents on AWS, get instant feedback on a live leaderboard, and compete in a game-show-style finale. Cisco is one of the clearest examples of what this looks like at scale. In 2025, Hemanth V, a Cisco software engineer, went from an internal Cisco event to being crowned the first AWS AI League Champion at AWS re:Invent 2025. In 2026, 1,200 Cisco engineers competed in an AWS AI League tournament at Cisco Transformation Fest 4.0. The winner, Nishanth Aluhonnu, earned a full event pass to AWS re:Invent 2026 in Las Vegas. In this post, we share how Cisco and AWS used Cisco Transformation Fest and AWS AI League to build a lasting culture of learning by doing. We previously covered this program in From theory to delivery: How Atos upskilled 400 engineers in agentic AI , and here we look at Cisco’s experience. We walk through Cisco’s journey, share technical lessons from the 2026 winning agent, and explain how your organization can host its own AWS AI League. What is AWS AI League? AWS AI League helps organizations build advanced AI skills through competition. Each league follows three steps: Learn – A hands-on, 2-hour workshop led by AWS experts introduces the tools and the challenge. Build – Participants experiment at their own pace and submit to a live leaderboard, with an automated evaluator giving real-time feedback after each submission. Compete – Top finalists take the stage in a live, game-show-style grand finale. Although AWS AI League offers multiple use cases, at Cisco it offered the following two challenges: Agentic AI challenge – Participants build agents with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore , a platform to build, connect, and optimize agents at scale with any framework or model. The agents move through a maze-like grid, solving challenges on the way to a treasure chest. The challenges map to real-world tasks such as handling inappropriate content, running code, retrieving information from the web, and extracting structured data. Builders can choose models for supervisor and sub-agents and add tools such as AgentCore memory, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore , and AWS Lambda Event Functions . Builders use Amazon Bedrock Guardrails to apply safety controls to their agents. Model customization challenge – Participants fine-tune models in Amazon SageMaker Studio using the latest training recipes. The challenge awards points when an automated evaluator rates a participant’s customized model as more accurate and comprehensive than a reference model on the specific tasks in the competition. Finalists are scored on time efficiency, accuracy, agent planning, and token consumption efficiency. title: Keep inference running through regional capacity shortfalls with cross-Region inference routing in Amazon SageMaker AI
abstract: Serving a model from more than one AWS Region is a well-established pattern for highly available inference: when one Region runs short of GPU capacity, requests move to another. The pattern is simple to describe and hard to operate. Until now, if you served models on Amazon SageMaker AI managed endpoints, cross-Region routing was a piece you still had to build yourself. Today, we’re introducing cross-Region inference routing in Amazon SageMaker AI. It uses a new resource, the inference router, that gives your application one invocation path across the endpoints and inference components you already run, in one or more AWS Regions and AWS accounts. You register the destinations that serve a model, and your application invokes the router instead of a specific endpoint. The router keeps requests in its own Region while the local destination is healthy, shifts new requests to another registered destination when it isn’t, and returns traffic gradually after recovery. In this post, we explain how cross-Region inference routing decides where each request runs, walk through an example with one model in two Regions, and cover monitoring, limits, and what you pay. For a cross-account deployment that serves several models, see How Salesforce is advancing global-scale model serving with cross-Region inference routing in Amazon SageMaker AI . When one Region runs short of capacity A SageMaker AI endpoint runs in one AWS Region and one account. When autoscaling can’t add instances of the type your endpoint needs, requests throttle and time out, even when the same model has spare capacity in another Region. To use that capacity, your application must detect a struggling endpoint and switch Regions, decide which errors are safe to retry without running the model twice, move traffic back after recovery without flapping, and manage access to endpoints in other accounts. That code sits on the critical path of every request, and every team serving models across Regions maintains its own version of it. How cross-Region inference routing works Cross-Region inference routing is based on a few core ideas: You decide where your model might run – For each model, you choose which endpoints and inference components the router might use. SageMaker AI decides which destination serves each request – The router prefers its own Region and shifts new requests to another destination only when the local one can’t serve reliably. Your endpoints stay the same – You deploy endpoints as you do today, with the same models, configurations, instance pools, and autoscaling. Direct InvokeEndpoint calls keep working, and the router passes InferenceId and CustomAttributes through, as InvokeEndpoint does. You can see every decision – Each real-time response tells you which destination served the request and why. A few terms describe the pieces: Inference router – A Regional SageMaker AI resource in your account that your application invokes. Routing target – A name for one logical model on a router, such as fraud-model . A router can hold many routing targets, and each fails over independently of the others. Destination – A real-time endpoint, inference component, or asynchronous endpoint registered under a routing target, identified by its full Amazon Resource Name (ARN), which tells the router its Region and account. A routing target holds either real-time destinations, which can mix endpoints and inference components across Regions and accounts, or asynchronous endpoints only. Local destination – A destination in the router’s Region, preferred while it’s healthy. Routing reason – A value returned with each real-time response that explains where the request went and why. The Region you create the router in is its local Region. To prefer a different Region, create a router there. title: Protect agent tool calls with Skyflow and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway
abstract: In this post, we show how Skyflow and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway keep sensitive data out of the tools your AI agents call, and out of the model context those tools feed. We add Skyflow Detect to Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway as a request and response interceptor . The Skyflow interceptor de-identifies data before it reaches a tool, restores it before the agent reads the result, and replaces documents with clean copies before the agent opens them. Your agents and tools don’t change. Skyflow is available in AWS Marketplace, and the interceptor is open source on GitHub. Agents act through tools, and tools move data Agents have moved from answering questions to taking action, and they take action through tools: Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers, SaaS APIs, document stores, and web search. Every agent tool call is a data flow. Most enterprise controls cover what goes into and comes out of the model. Far fewer cover what an agent sends to its tools or what those tools send back. That gap shows up in three ways: Sensitive data leaves through tool arguments. The model writes the arguments from everything in its context, including details the tool doesn’t need. Ask an agent about a customer, and the customer’s name, account number, or email goes straight into a query to a third-party server. That server sits outside your AWS account and your compliance scope. Sensitive data comes back in tool results. Scraped web pages, CRM records, and case notes land in the model’s context, memory, traces, and logs. This happens even when the task never needed them. Documents bypass text inspection. Document tools such as Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3), Box, and Google Drive return a signed URL, not text. A filter that inspects strings sees a link and lets it through, and the agent then opens the original file. Patching each agent doesn’t scale across teams and frameworks, and it can’t reach third-party tools. The controls need to sit where every tool call passes, so authorization, content safety, and data protection apply the same way to every agent and tool. AgentCore Gateway is that place. It fronts every tool an agent uses, whatever framework or model the agent runs on. It does more than route that traffic. With AgentCore Gateway interceptors, you can run your own code, as an AWS Lambda function, on every call that passes through it. A request interceptor sees each call before it reaches a tool, and a response interceptor sees each result before it reaches the agent. Either one can inspect the payload, rewrite it, or block the call. That makes the gateway a natural place to add data protection alongside Policy and Guardrails. This single control, attached once, covers every agent and every tool behind the gateway, without any change to agent or tool code. Example: A dispute-resolution agent at a large European bank Consider a large European bank with retail and corporate banking operations and strict data-residency obligations. Its operations teams are adopting agents to investigate card disputes. An analyst asks the agent to look into a disputed transaction. The agent searches the web for the merchant, then pulls the dispute case note from Amazon S3 to summarize it. Without protection, three things happen: The model builds the search query from everything in context. The search provider receives ‘Mateo Jackson dispute AnyCompany Electronics London’. That’s the customer’s name, sent to a third party, for a search that only needed the merchant. Scraped merchant pages bring unrelated personal data into the model’s context. The agent reads the original case note, with the customer’s full name, email, phone number, and card details. With the Skyflow interceptor on the gateway, the same workflow plays out differently: The search provider receives ‘[NAME_AJbrIud] dispute AnyCompany Electronics London’, where [NAME_AJbrIud] is a reversible vault token. abstract: On October 16, 2026, I delivered the second Annual Margaret Levi Lecture in Political Economy in conjunction with the AI and History conference at Johns Hopkins University in Baltimore. This is my original lecture as written, which incorporates material from many pieces I’ve written over the years. As delivered, I departed significantly from the script, as you can see from the embedded video below or the transcript that you can see at the link above. It’s an honor to give a lecture in Margaret Levi’s name. I’ve been asked to reflect on the changes in the political economy of Silicon Valley throughout my 40-plus year career in and about it, and I can’t imagine a better framing for my remarks than Margaret’s vision. Margaret understood that advances in our ability to work together are essential to a better future. Cooperation is the human superpower. She also asks what happens when the systems of cooperation we have constructed over time stop holding up their end of the bargain. That is very much the question that Silicon Valley is facing today. An industry that pioneered advances in collective intelligence at scale used to engender love from its customers because of the way it solved new problems in their lives. It now too often inspires fear and loathing. How did things go so wrong? The web I thought we were building in 1993 But let me start with my own history. I started my company more than 40 years ago with a $500 initial investment. We took in no venture capital, and we built a business that now generates hundreds of millions of dollars in profitable annual revenue, funded by customers who love our products and pay us for them. We got there the slow way, through steady organic growth. That is quite anathema to the rush to the top of whatever appears to be the latest hill that seems to characterize Silicon Valley today. Even when climbing that hill traps a company at a local maximum, the hope is to get to payday before the industry moves on to the next hill. My original corporate goal was stated as simply “Interesting work for interesting people.” That evolved into two principles: “Change the world by spreading the knowledge of innovators,” and “Create more value than you capture.” Those principles shaped not only my company but what I expected the internet to be. When we launched GNN , the Global Network Navigator, in 1993, it was the first web portal and the first ad-supported site on the World Wide Web, and for two years it was the place people went to find other sites. What we built was a machine for pointing you at the best of what other people had made, and then getting out of your way. Even our idea of advertising was not what you think of today. It was inspired by direct mail advertising, where you’d read articles in a print magazine or look at accompanying ads, and then you’d call an 800 number or circle a number on a “bingo card” that you’d send in to the publisher so that the advertiser could send you a brochure. I realized that the web would be a good replacement for that awkward system, that every company ought to have its own website that provided more information about its products and services. What we invented was not the “grab your attention” kind of advertising. It was all about utility, and sharing information that customers really wanted and needed. In short, it was the commercial web, which no one any longer thinks of as advertising, even though it is the most durable and useful kind. The commercial web was only a small part of what the web became. The web was the playground of amateurs, not entrepreneurs.
